summary: OSPFv3 used IPsec as its only way to authenticate protocol packets, unlike OSPFv2, IS-IS, RIP, and RIPng. This document adds an authentication trailer mechanism for OSPFv3.

eli5.summary: A routing protocol could only check IDs through one special machine. This lets it attach an ID check directly to its messages instead.

questions: what is the ospfv3 authentication trailer
which hash algorithms does ospfv3 authentication use
subtitle: A way to authenticate OSPFv3 packets with a trailer and a keyed hash, so routers need not depend on IPsec.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 relied only on IPsec to authenticate protocol packets, which is hard to configure in some environments and gives no replay protection with manual keys.
tldr.mechanism: Each OSPFv3 packet gets an Authentication Trailer with a security association ID, a 64-bit strictly increasing sequence number and an HMAC digest computed with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6506 with clarifications and corrections, such as the key preparation fix and the omitted checksums.

today: RFC 7166 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 6506, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Per its IANA section, registry references that pointed to RFC 6506 now point to this document.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Needs Its Own Authentication
sections.content:
Unlike OSPFv2, OSPFv3 has no AuType or Authentication fields in its headers. It relies on the IPsec protocols AH and ESP for integrity, authentication and confidentiality, as described in RFC 4552. In some environments, for example Mobile Ad Hoc Networks, IPsec is difficult to configure and maintain.

The reason for manual keys is that OSPFv3 adjacencies are formed one-to-many, while most key management mechanisms assume one-to-one communication. With manual keying, RFC 4552 provides no protection against replay attacks, which leaves several vulnerabilities discussed in RFC 6039. It is also hard for routers to spot and prioritize packet types such as Hello when they are wrapped in ESP-NULL.

This document defines a mechanism that works much like the OSPFv2 one in RFC 5709 and solves both problems. It obsoletes RFC 6506 and makes seven changes, including explicit omission of the LLS block checksum, removal of advice to use an expired key, a corrected key preparation step, per packet type sequence number checking, and guidance for a backward-compatible transition mode.
sections.eli5: The old way to sign routing messages needed a complicated sealed envelope that is hard to set up. This gives each message a simple signature that is easy to check.

sections.title: The Authentication Trailer
sections.content:
To authenticate without IPsec, OSPFv3 routers append a data block, the Authentication Trailer (AT), to the end of the packet. Its length is not counted in the OSPFv3 packet length but is counted in the IPv6 payload length. If a Link-Local Signaling (LLS) block is present, as signaled by the L-bit in the Options field of Hello and Database Description packets, the LLS block sits before the trailer and is included in the digest.

A new AT-bit in the OSPFv3 Options field tells neighbors that the packets on the link include a trailer. Routers MUST set it in Hello and Database Description packets, and other packet types use the setting remembered in the neighbor data structure.

Two details differ from OSPFv2. The OSPFv3 header checksum and the LLS block checksum are neither calculated nor verified. And the IPv6 source address is covered by the digest. OSPFv3 learns the source address from Hello packets, so without this a man-in-the-middle could change it.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a signed tag stapled to its end. A flag at the front tells the receiver to look for the tag.

sections.title: Security Associations and Keys
sections.content:
An OSPFv3 Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters shared between legitimate speakers. It has a 16-bit SA ID chosen by the operator, an authentication algorithm, an authentication key, and four times: KeyStartAccept, KeyStartGenerate, KeyStopGenerate and KeyStopAccept. The algorithm is never sent on the wire. The receiver finds the SA from the SA ID in the packet.

The four times allow smooth key changes. KeyStartAccept SHOULD be less than KeyStartGenerate, and KeyStopGenerate SHOULD be less than KeyStopAccept. A new key's KeyStartGenerate MUST be less than or equal to the old key's KeyStopGenerate. Unspecified start times default to 0 and unspecified stop times to infinity.

Key storage SHOULD survive restarts. If the last key on an interface expires, the operator SHOULD be told and the packet MUST NOT be sent unauthenticated.
sections.eli5: Each router keeps a numbered keyring with dates saying when each key may be used, so the keys can be swapped without the network falling apart.

sections.title: The Trailer Format
sections.content:
The trailer starts with a 16-octet fixed part followed by the variable-length digest. Authentication Type is 16 bits: 0 is reserved and 1 means HMAC cryptographic authentication. Auth Data Len is the total trailer length in octets, fixed header plus digest. Reserved SHOULD be 0 when sending and MUST be ignored on receipt. The SA ID maps to the algorithm and key. Receivers should not guess the algorithm from the digest size, since later algorithms may share the same size.

The Cryptographic Sequence Number is 64 bits and strictly increasing. It MUST be incremented for every packet sent. On receipt it MUST be greater than the number in the last accepted packet of the same OSPFv3 packet type from that neighbor, or the packet is treated as a replay and dropped. The check is per type because prioritization can reorder packets of different types.

Routers MUST preserve the strictly increasing property across cold restarts. One suggested method is to use the high-order 32 bits as a boot or wrap count. If the 64-bit number could ever wrap, all keys MUST be reset first.
sections.eli5: The tag has a number that goes up with every message. If a message arrives with an old number, the router knows someone is replaying a copy and throws it away.

sections.title: Algorithms and the Digest
sections.content:
The digest uses HMAC with the SHA family. Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256, SHOULD support HMAC-SHA-1, and MAY support HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. HMAC-SHA-256 MUST be the default.

The key is first prepared. The authentication key K gets the two-octet OSPFv3 Cryptographic Protocol ID appended, giving Ks, to prevent cross-protocol replay between protocols that share keys. Ks is then padded with zeros or hashed so the working key Ko is exactly L octets long, where L is the hash length.

The digest field is first filled with Apad, which holds the IPv6 source address followed by repeats of the value 0x878FE1F3. The inner hash is H(Ko XOR Ipad || OSPFv3 packet), where the packet includes any LLS block and the trailer. The outer hash is H(Ko XOR Opad || First-Hash), and the result becomes the authentication data. Ipad is 0x36 and Opad is 0x5c, each repeated B times.
sections.eli5: The router mixes the message with a secret key through a scrambling machine twice. Only someone who knows the key can get the same scrambled result.

sections.title: Verifying a Received Packet
sections.content:
A router learns that a trailer is used from the AT-bit in Hello and Database Description packets. It finds the trailer after the OSPFv3 packet, and after the LLS block if the L-bit says there is one. Routers MUST at least check the L-bit and use the LLS length to find the trailer.

If the trailer is configured on a link, Hello and Database Description packets with the AT-bit clear are dropped. A packet is also dropped if its SA is not found or is outside its accept times, or if its sequence number is less than or equal to the last one from that neighbor for the same packet type. A replay SHOULD be logged.

The router saves the received digest, puts Apad into the field, recomputes the digest and compares. A mismatch means the packet MUST be discarded and an error event SHOULD be logged. After success, the router MUST store the 64-bit sequence number for that packet type from the neighbor.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the flag, finds the tag, makes sure the number is new, and redoes the scrambling. If its answer does not match the tag, the message is thrown away.

sections.title: Migration and Compatibility
sections.content:
All routers on a link SHOULD move to authentication at the same time. A mismatch in SA ID, Authentication Type or digest prevents an adjacency from forming. Splitting a multi-access link using different Interface Instance IDs is possible but needs at least one router that peers with both groups. That gives sub-optimal routing and extra complexity.

A router MAY offer a transition mode that includes the trailer in transmitted packets but does not verify received ones. In this mode it sets the AT-bit, still calculates the header and LLS checksums so routers without authentication do not drop the packets, authenticates packets that carry the AT-bit or come from a neighbor that previously did, and accepts packets without the AT-bit as coming from unauthenticated routers, validating their checksums.
sections.eli5: It is best if everyone starts signing their messages on the same day. If not, there is a temporary mode where a router signs its messages but still reads unsigned ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism does not provide confidentiality, because a routing protocol carries nothing that must be kept secret. It authenticates that a packet came from a router that has access to the authentication key, not which specific router sent it. The RFC says it addresses all the issues identified in RFC 6039 and RFC 6506.

Keys SHOULD be long and random, and it is RECOMMENDED that they incorporate at least 128 pseudorandom bits. Management systems SHOULD accept hexadecimal key input. Networks that use transition mode may be exposed to unauthenticated data during the transition. The RFC says plainly that the mechanism is not perfect and does not need to be, but that it significantly raises the effort needed to attack OSPFv3.
sections.eli5: The signature proves a message came from someone with the secret key, but it does not hide the message. Pick long, random secrets so nobody can guess them.

fields.name: Authentication Type
fields.desc: 0 is reserved; 1 means HMAC cryptographic authentication.

fields.name: Auth Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the whole trailer in octets, fixed header plus digest.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: SHOULD be 0 on send; MUST be ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Security Association ID
fields.desc: Maps to the authentication algorithm and key.

fields.name: Cryptographic Sequence Number (High-Order 32 Bits)
fields.desc: High half of the 64-bit strictly increasing sequence number.

fields.name: Cryptographic Sequence Number (Low-Order 32 Bits)
fields.desc: Low half of the sequence number.
